migrationNotes: Spine: put a stopwatch in the corridor. Divide ground by time for average speed, add the direction for average velocity, then watch the two come apart on a trip that turns round and on a trip made of unequal stretches.

Left out of the lesson (still in the course): phys-speed-and-direction-hook, -sign, -4. The faded example and the old hook are covered by other items; -4 (multiple choice) was replaced by the numeric phys-speed-and-direction-slow-half.

lesson.title: Speed and direction

lead.text: Take the dash from the opener: 20 metres in 4 seconds. Share the ground out over the time and you get 5 metres for every second. A number like that is the average speed of the trip, found by dividing the distance travelled by the time it took.

The unit follows from the sum. Metres divided by seconds gives metres per second, written m/s, so 5 m/s means 5 metres of ground for each second that passes. The word average matters. A cyclist who dawdled at the start and sprinted at the end could cover the same 20 metres in the same 4 seconds, and the sum would still give 5 m/s. It describes the trip as a whole and says nothing about any single moment.

afterFigure.text: Here is a second example, a runner who covers 12 metres in 3 seconds. Dividing gives 12 ÷ 3 = 4 m/s. Stretch the same 12 metres over 6 seconds and the answer halves to 2 m/s, which matches what you would see, because the runner is moving more slowly. The distance in this sum is the total path length from the last lesson, so it never carries a sign. That leaves open what to do when the direction matters.

lead.text: A rover drives straight for 6 seconds and covers 18 metres. It need not keep one pace the whole way.

reveal.text: You divided the distance by the time. That is an average: the rover may have been faster and slower along the way.

lead.text: Average speed forgets which way you went. That suits a pedometer, but the last lesson showed that direction matters, because displacement keeps it as a sign. Divide the displacement by the time instead of the distance and you get the average velocity.

A cyclist whose displacement is +8 m in 2 s has an average velocity of +4 m/s. A cyclist who ends up 9 metres behind the start after 3 seconds has an average velocity of −9 ÷ 3 = −3 m/s. The sign says which way along the line the trip went, and the number says how fast.

afterFigure.text: On a straight trip that never turns round, the displacement and the distance have the same size. The average speed is then the size of the average velocity, and the only difference is the sign. That is why speed is never negative while velocity can be. The two come apart once a trip doubles back, and a later screen looks at that.

lead.text: A cart rolls to the left. Left is the negative direction, so the displacement has a minus sign.

Now let the trip turn round. Suppose you walk 30 m to a shop and straight back, and the whole round trip takes 20 s. The distance is 30 + 30 = 60 m, so the average speed is 60 ÷ 20 = 3 m/s. That matches how brisk the walk felt.

The displacement tells a different story. You finished where you started, so finishing minus starting is 0 m. The average velocity is 0 ÷ 20 = 0 m/s. The way out counts as positive and the way back as negative, so in displacement they cancel. In distance they cannot cancel, because every stretch adds.

afterFigure.text: This is the sense in which velocity and speed differ. Speed asks how much ground is covered each second. Velocity asks how fast the position is changing in a particular direction, so a trip that ends at its start has an average velocity of zero no matter how fast it went. From here on we keep both, and use whichever the question needs.

cases.label: Shop and back: 60 m in 20 s

steps.headline: A trolley goes 15 m right in 3 s, then 5 m left in 2 s. Find both averages.

workedSteps.text: Add the lengths of the stretches and add the times. Average speed divides the total distance by the total time.
Displacement is the net move, with right positive.
Average velocity divides the displacement by the same total time.

lead.text: A runner heads out along a straight road and then comes straight back to the marker where the run began.

reveal.text: The finish equals the start, so the displacement is zero. Distance and displacement part company on a return trip.

lead.text: Many trips come in stretches at different paces, and the average for the whole trip needs care. Suppose a jogger covers 10 m in 2 s, then slows and covers the next 10 m in 8 s. The first stretch is 5 m/s and the second is 1.25 m/s. It is tempting to average those two numbers and get about 3.1 m/s.

That answer is too high. The jogger spent four times as long on the slow stretch as on the fast one, so the slow stretch should count for more. Go back to the definition and use the totals: 20 m of ground in 2 + 8 = 10 s gives 20 ÷ 10 = 2 m/s. The rule is the same every time, the total distance over the total time, whatever the stretches looked like.

afterFigure.text: The same rule works for average velocity: the total displacement over the total time. When a trip is made of stretches, add up the stretches first and divide once at the end.

lead.text: A cyclist rides two equal stretches, but the second takes longer than the first.

reveal.text: The whole trip is 24 m in 8 s. The mean of the two stretch speeds is 4 m/s, which gives too much weight to the faster stretch.

lesson.orientation: Use elapsed time to distinguish average speed from average velocity.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Last lesson's corridor had no clock in it. Put one there. A friend stands at a mark 20 metres from the door with a stopwatch, and you set off from the door on a bicycle at a steady pace. They start the watch as you go and stop it as you pass them. It reads 4 seconds.

That reading adds something new. The corridor tells us how much ground the trip covered. The stopwatch tells us how long it took. Put together, they say how fast you went. They also let us compare trips: a friend who covered the 20 metres in 5 seconds was slower.

Things get more interesting once the trip turns round. Cycle to the far mark and come straight back to the door, and your friend can say you were moving quickly and also that you ended up where you began. Both remarks are true, and they come from two different calculations. Sorting them out starts with the straight dash.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find average speed and average velocity from a trip, and say when they differ.

recap.keyIdea: Average speed is total distance over total time. Average velocity is total displacement over total time, so it carries a sign and is zero on a trip that ends where it began.

blocks.text: You turned 20 m in 4 s into 5 m for each second. You then saw that a return trip has an average velocity of 0 even though ground was covered, and that the average for a trip made of stretches comes from the totals.

recap.nextHook: A table of positions and times is slow to read. Next we draw position against time and see what the shape of the line says about speed and direction.

questions.prompt: A rover covers 18 m in 6 s without reversing. What is its average speed in m/s?
hints: Use total distance and elapsed time.
Divide distance by time.
Share the travelled distance equally across the elapsed seconds.
questions.onCorrect: 3 m/s. Average speed is total distance divided by total time.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies the distance by the time. Speed is distance shared out over time, so divide.
That divides time by distance. Speed is distance per unit of time.

questions.prompt: A cart's displacement is −12 m over 3 s. Find its average velocity in m/s.
hints: Velocity keeps the direction of displacement.
Divide the signed displacement by elapsed time.
Divide the displacement magnitude by duration and keep its negative sign.
questions.onCorrect: −4 m/s. Velocity keeps the sign of the displacement, so a leftward move gives a negative velocity.

misconceptions.feedback: The size is right, but the cart moved left. Velocity keeps the sign of the displacement.
That multiplies by the time. Divide the displacement by it.

questions.prompt: A runner goes 10 m from a marker and returns to that marker in a total of 5 s. Find the average velocity in m/s.
hints: Use the final and initial positions.
A return to the same point leaves no displacement.
Divide that displacement by the total time.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The displacement is zero, so average velocity is 0/5 = 0 m/s.

questions.onCorrect: 0 m/s. The runner ends where they began, so the displacement is zero whatever the distance run.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the average speed for the out leg only. Velocity uses the displacement over the whole trip.
That divides the distance there and back by the time. Velocity uses displacement, not distance.

questions.prompt: A robot travels 6 m in 2 s, then 6 m in 4 s. What is its average speed for the whole trip?
hints: Combine distances and times before dividing.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The whole trip is 12 m in 6 s, giving 2 m/s. The slower section lasts longer.

questions.onCorrect: 2 m/s. Add the distances, add the times, then divide. Averaging the two speeds would over-weight the fast stretch.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the mean of the two stretch speeds. The slower stretch lasts longer, so it should count for more.
That is the speed of the first stretch only. Use the whole trip.

questions.prompt: A conveyor moves a parcel 42 m along a straight path in 7 s. What is its average speed in m/s?
hints: Identify the path length and duration.
Use distance divided by time.
Find how many metres correspond to one second.
questions.onCorrect: 6 m/s. Distance divided by time, with the path length and the duration both read from the problem.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies the two numbers. Divide the distance by the time.
That divides time by distance. Speed is distance per second.

questions.prompt: A moving object returns to its start. Which average must be zero over the complete trip?
hints: Ask which average uses displacement.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Only average velocity must be zero, because displacement is zero. The distance travelled is positive.

questions.onCorrect: Average velocity. A return to the start makes the displacement zero; the distance travelled stays positive.

misconceptions.feedback: Average speed uses distance, and the distance run is not zero. Which average uses displacement?
Only one of them uses displacement. The other uses the distance, which cannot be zero for a trip.

questions.prompt: Cycling at a steady pace, you cover 20 m in 4 s. How many metres do you cover each second?
hints: Share the 20 m equally across the 4 seconds.
Each second covers the same distance.
How many 4s fit into 20?
questions.onCorrect: 5 m/s. Sharing a distance equally over the time taken is the idea behind every speed.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies the two numbers. Each second covers less than the whole 20 m, so divide.

questions.prompt: A cart's displacement is −10 m over 5 s. What is its average velocity in m/s?
hints: Which quantity is on the top of the division: distance or displacement?
Divide the signed displacement by the elapsed time.
Keep the minus sign through the division.
questions.onCorrect: −2 m/s. Dividing by a positive time keeps the sign of the displacement.

misconceptions.feedback: The size is right, but velocity carries the direction. The displacement was negative.
That multiplies by the time. Divide the displacement by it.

questions.prompt: Why are the two averages different for this trip?
hints: Read each choice against the situation before you answer.

acceptedIdeas: The trolley turned back, so the displacement is smaller than the distance.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The trolley turned back, so the displacement is smaller than the distance.

choices.label: The trolley turned back, so the displacement is smaller than the distance.
Velocity is always half of speed.
The times are different for each average.

questions.onCorrect: Turning back shrinks the displacement but not the distance. Same time, different top line.

misconceptions.feedback: There is no fixed ratio. The two averages differ here because of what goes on top of the division.
Both averages use the same total time. Look at the quantity divided by it.

questions.prompt: A walker goes 30 m east in 5 s, then 6 m west in 1 s. With east positive, what is the average velocity over the whole trip, in m/s?
hints: Subtract the westward distance from the eastward distance to get the net move.
Add the two times to get the whole trip's time.
Divide the net move by the total time.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Displacement 30 − 6 = +24 m over 6 s gives +4 m/s.

questions.onCorrect: +4 m/s. Net displacement over total time: the westward stretch partly cancels the eastward one.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides the whole path length by the time. That is the average speed, not the velocity.
The walker finishes east of the start, so the net movement is eastward.

questions.prompt: A cyclist rides 12 m in 2 s, then a further 12 m in 6 s. What is the average speed for the whole trip, in m/s?
hints: How much ground does the whole trip cover?
How long does the whole trip take, with both stretches together?
Divide the total ground by the total time.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The trip is 12 + 12 = 24 m in 2 + 6 = 8 s, so the average speed is 24 ÷ 8 = 3 m/s.

questions.onCorrect: 3 m/s. Add the distances, add the times, then divide once: 24 m over 8 s.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the mean of the two stretch speeds. The slow stretch lasts three times as long, so it counts for more.
That divides the time by the distance. Speed is distance per second.

citations.claim: Average speed is total distance divided by the time taken, in metres per second.

Average velocity is displacement divided by time, so it carries a sign; speed is its size on a straight trip.
A displacement of −12 m over 3 s gives an average velocity of −4 m/s.
On a return trip the displacement is zero, so the average velocity is zero while the average speed is not.
For 15 m right in 3 s then 5 m left in 2 s, the average speed is 4 m/s and the average velocity is +2 m/s.
A runner who returns to the start has zero displacement, so the average velocity is 0 m/s.
The average speed of a trip is its total distance over its total time, not the mean of its stretch speeds.
A cyclist covering 12 m in 2 s and 12 m in 6 s has an average speed of 24 ÷ 8 = 3 m/s.
The trip is 12 + 12 = 24 m in 2 + 6 = 8 s, so the average speed is 24 ÷ 8 = 3 m/s.
The displacement is zero, so average velocity is 0/5 = 0 m/s.
Only average velocity must be zero, because displacement is zero. The distance travelled is positive.
The trolley turned back, so the displacement is smaller than the distance.
Displacement 30 − 6 = +24 m over 6 s gives +4 m/s.
